title: Everything but the direction
intro: The level above named the ten perturbations and the two figures they appear in. This one takes the apparatus apart: how the norm being matched is computed at each layer and position, what each of the four dictionaries was built to contain and to exclude, and what the six panels and the story control do and do not settle.

chapters.title: What a control has to match
chapters.body:
The intervention as run in these experiments works position by position. At each token position, across layers L38 to L54, the ten most strongly activated [[j-lens-vector]]s are identified, the [[residual-stream]]'s projection onto each is zeroed, and the forward pass continues ([[j-space-ablation]]).

The piece removed is therefore not a fixed vector. Its size depends on how much of the activation at that position happened to lie along those particular ten directions. A position where the workspace is heavily loaded loses a larger vector than one where it is close to empty.

That is what the matching has to track. Each control's perturbation is scaled separately at every layer and every token position, to the norm the ablation would have removed there ([[matched-norm-controls]]). Across the whole run, only the choice of direction varies.

One detail of the ablation carries into what the controls are being asked about. Any lens vector whose token already sat among the ten most likely outputs of a clean forward pass is skipped ([[ablation-report-exemption]]), so the intervention targets content the model holds rather than words it was about to emit. The appendix does not state whether the dictionary controls carry an equivalent carve-out.

The layer band is narrower than the ablation strengths used elsewhere in the section. L38–54 covers roughly the first third of the [[workspace-layers]], layer numbers being percentages of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). Raising $k$ or moving to later layers damages coherence before the register changes, and on Haiku 4.5 of the [[claude-model-family]] coherence breaks first at every setting tried ([[ablation-coherence-limit]]).

A matched norm buys one thing precisely. It removes the explanation that the model was simply hit harder. It does not make the perturbations equivalent in what they destroy: an equal-sized nudge along a direction the model barely uses costs it nothing.

chapters.title: Features chosen for not being in the workspace
chapters.body:
The dictionary controls are built to a stated goal: banks of directions that resemble lens directions in everything except membership in the workspace ([[dictionary-control-battery]]).

The first bank takes decoder directions from a [[sparse-autoencoder]], which learns to decompose activations into sparsely active linear features. Its decoder directions are the nearest available thing to a large bank of model-native concept directions that were found without reference to the J-lens.

That independence is incomplete, and the paper has a statistic for the overlap. [[lens-kurtosis]] projects a feature's decoder direction through the [[j-lens-readout]], producing a score over the vocabulary, and measures the excess [[kurtosis]] of that distribution. A feature with high $\kappa$ is loaded disproportionately onto a small number of lens vectors. A feature with low $\kappa$ spreads diffusely across the vocabulary and aligns with no small set.

The second SAE bank is the bottom half by $\kappa$, sampled at random. The appendix reports that the distribution is heavy-tailed, and that the low-$\kappa$ bulk is dominated by syntactic and surface bookkeeping: a loop variable in a decrementing for-loop, the first digit of a page range in a citation, markdown section headers ([[bookkeeping-features]], [[fig-74]]). Their lens readouts bear no relation to what they appear to mean.

The high-$\kappa$ tail splits two ways. Some features name an abstract concept and fire when it is invoked ([[workspace-features]]); others fire just before the token they promote ([[motor-features]]).

So the two SAE banks differ in tightness. The low-kurtosis half is filtered against the workspace by construction. The full dictionary is not, and roughly 15 percent of features pass a kurtosis criterion at its peak layer once motor features are set aside ([[fig-75]]). A top-ten-aligned pick from the full bank can land on directions the paper itself counts as workspace directions.

chapters.title: The bank the model wrote itself
chapters.body:
The other two dictionaries hold no learned features at all. The raw bank is a collection of the model's own residual-stream states, recorded while it reads unrelated pretraining-style text.

The case for it is that these are real activations. They carry the scale, the covariance and the sparsity structure of what the model actually computes, which a random direction does not. The cost is that they carry whatever workspace content happened to be present when they were recorded.

The fourth bank subtracts that content. For each entry, [[gradient-pursuit]] solves greedily for a sparse nonnegative combination of $k=16$ lens vectors that reconstructs it well, and the entry is orthogonalized against that fit. The lens vectors are overcomplete and not orthogonal ([[sparse-subframe]]), so the greedy fit is not the same as taking the sixteen largest inner products; it tends to return a less redundant set. What the fit spans is the entry's [[j-space-component]], and what survives subtraction is the remainder ([[j-space-component-decomposition]]).

The size of what gets removed is small. The paper reports that the [[j-space]] component never accounts for more than 10 percent of activation variance at any layer, and that for [[concept-vector]]s the median is 6 to 7 percent. A J-stripped entry is therefore nearly the raw entry.

That is the design's point and also its limit. The two banks differ almost only in the piece the ablation removes, so a gap between them would isolate the effect of workspace content directly. No such gap is reported: both stay near baseline. The pair rules a possibility out rather than demonstrating anything. A bank of real activations does not flatten the reports, and the small amount of workspace content it carries is not what makes the difference.

chapters.title: Six panels, twelve bars
chapters.body:
[[fig-86]] plots the components rather than the summary. Its three columns are the three binary judgments that average into the [[experiential-language-score]], and its two rows are the stream-of-consciousness prompts and the direct [[experience-question-prompts]]. The figure shows where the average came from, which the main figures do not.

Twelve bars fill each panel: the unperturbed baseline, the ablation, and the ten controls. Bar length is the fraction of responses that one grader scored 1, on an axis from 0 to 100 percent, and the whiskers are [[wilson-interval]]s rather than normal-approximation ones. That choice does work here, because several bars sit near 5 percent, where a symmetric interval would extend below zero.

The ablation bar is shortest in all six panels, and in five of them the nearest control stands well clear of it. The exception is sensory vocabulary on the stream-of-consciousness prompts. There the full SAE dictionary at ten directions scores 19 percent against the ablation's 5 percent — close to a factor of four apart — and the two intervals still meet at their edges.

The figure offers no account of why that panel behaves differently. Two features of it are on the record. The sensory-vocabulary rubric is the strictest of the three, since it asks for words a person would use about their own body, so every bar in that column is pressed toward zero and the intervals are correspondingly wide relative to the gaps. And the full SAE dictionary is the only bank in the battery that is neither random, nor a complement of the workspace, nor filtered against workspace membership.

One limit of scope belongs with the result. The battery runs on Sonnet 4.5 alone. [[fig-25]] and [[fig-84]] cover Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 as well; this extended control set does not.

chapters.title: Changing the task instead of the direction
chapters.body:
The last control leaves the perturbation alone and changes what the model is asked to do. Under the same ablation, it writes short stories from six prompts, and two separate quantities are graded on the results.

Story craft is judged by an Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]] against one rubric, printed in the appendix as: "story_quality (0-10): Overall craft — is this a well-written short story? 10 = publishable-quality flash fiction: vivid, controlled, satisfying. 5 = competent but flat. 0 = broken or incoherent." The experiential judgments are the same three rubrics used elsewhere, in variants adapted to third-person stories rather than first-person reports.

The argument turns on the two quantities moving apart. A general collapse of writing ability would drag both down together. The paper reports that coherence is preserved, that quality falls only modestly, and that the rate of experiential language inside the stories still falls ([[story-writing-control]], [[fig-85]]).

Three qualifications sit against that. The text gives no number for either quantity, so "modestly" cannot be checked against the size of the experiential drop measured in the other figures. Both gradings come from the same grader model, so the separation depends on the craft rubric being indifferent to register; a grader that read detached prose as flat writing would have pulled the two together.

And the story prompts never ask for experiential writing. Its presence at baseline is incidental, which cuts both ways. A drop measured from an unrequested baseline is a claim about the model's propensity rather than about its compliance with an instruction, but the baseline it drops from is whatever those six prompts happened to produce ([[experiential-report-flattening]], [[experiential-reports]]).
